walkthroughs.body_html:
From William I's reign, Jews provided money-lending barred to Christians.

They were taxed heavily and attacked — like in York 1190 when 150 died at Clifford's Tower. In 1290 Edward I issued the Edict of Expulsion — Jews could not legally return until 1656 under Cromwell.

From the 1200s the Hanseatic League used a riverside base called the Steelyard.

In the 1330s Edward III invited Flemish weavers to boost the wool trade. They settled in East Anglia and Kent, helping turn England into a cloth exporter.

The 1598 Edict of Nantes gave French Protestants toleration. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685.

About 50,000 Huguenots fled to England, settling in Spitalfields and Soho. They brought silk-weaving, banking and the word 'refugee' itself.

mcqs.q: How did Anglo-Saxons come to dominate post-Roman Britain?
options: A mix of migration from northern Germany and Denmark, settlement and intermarriage, and cultural absorption of Romano-British populations — not simple invasion and replacement.
William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.
Anglo-Saxons came as refugees fleeing the Vikings.
Anglo-Saxons invaded Britain and wiped out all the Romano-British inhabitants.

mcqs.q: Why did Caribbean migrants come to Britain in 1948 on the Windrush?
options: Windrush migrants were illegal immigrants from outside the empire.
Britain faced post-war labour shortages; the 1948 British Nationality Act gave Commonwealth citizens UK residency rights and Caribbean migrants answered the call to rebuild.
Windrush migrants came as refugees from Caribbean famines.
Anglo-Saxons came as refugees fleeing the Vikings.

mcqs.q: Why did William of Normandy claim the English throne in 1066?
options: William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.
He claimed Edward the Confessor had promised him the throne in 1051 and that Harold Godwinson had sworn an oath to support that claim in 1064.
William invaded because he was the strongest king in Europe and wanted more land.
Anglo-Saxons came as refugees fleeing the Vikings.
